title: Accusative 2: Feminine Things Change

title: Accusative 3: Two Kinds of WHAT

title: Accusative 7: Many Things Stay the Same

title: Adjective Agreement 1: Hard Stems
description: Russian adjectives change shape to match the gender and number of their noun. Today we drill the four hard-stem endings: -ый for masculine, -ая for feminine, -ое for neuter, -ые for plural.

title: Adjective Agreement 2: Soft Stems
description: A small but high-frequency family of Russian adjectives takes a parallel set of soft endings: -ий for masculine, -яя for feminine, -ее for neuter, -ие for plural. Words today: синий, последний, домашний, утренний, ранний.

title: Adjective Agreement 3: Mixed Stems
description: A third class of adjectives looks like a mix of hard and soft endings: хороший, русский, маленький, большой. Today we drill their forms as a unit; Lesson 4 returns to the spelling rules that make them look mixed.

title: Adjective Agreement 4: Spelling Rule Effects
description: The mechanism behind Lesson 3's mixed-looking forms. Three spelling rules cover almost every surface oddity: no -ы after velar / husher, no unstressed -о after husher, stressed masculine -ой instead of -ый.

title: Adjective Agreement 5: Chains in 'Это' and 'У меня' Sentences
titleEnglish: Adjective Agreement 5: Chains in 'Это' and 'У меня' Sentences
description: Production practice. Build full sentences with adjective + noun chains in the two highest-frequency A1 frames: 'Это [adj] [noun]' for identification and 'У меня [adj] [noun]' for possession. Mixes hard, soft, and mixed-stem classes from Lessons 1 to 4.

title: Adjective Agreement 6: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis. Mixed quiz across all five prior rules: hard stems, soft stems, mixed stems, the three spelling rules, and the chain frames. Pattern recognition asks which rule produced each form.

title: Genitive 1: Saying What's Missing
description: Masculine nouns add -а in the genitive (-я for soft stems ending in -й or -ь). The genitive is used after нет to say something is absent.

title: Genitive 2: Feminine Endings (-ы and -и)
description: Feminine nouns ending in -а take -ы in the genitive (-и after к, г, х, ш, ж, щ, ч). Feminine nouns ending in -я take -и.

title: Genitive 3: Neuter Endings (-а and -я)
description: Neuter nouns ending in -о take -а in the genitive. Neuter nouns ending in -е take -я.

title: Genitive 4: 'There Is No X' Across All Genders
titleEnglish: Genitive 4: 'There Is No X' Across All Genders
description: The нет + genitive construction works the same way for all three genders. Today you mix masculine, feminine, and neuter together.

title: Genitive 5: есть vs нет
description: After есть the noun stays in the nominative. After нет it shifts into the genitive. Drill the alternation.

title: Genitive 6: After Prepositions (без, у, для, из, от)
titleEnglish: Genitive 6: After Prepositions (без, у, для, из, от)
description: Five common prepositions (без, у, для, из, от) require the genitive case. Same gender rules apply.

title: Genitive 7: Mixed Review (All Triggers, All Genders)
titleEnglish: Genitive 7: Mixed Review (All Triggers, All Genders)
description: Synthesis lesson. Mixes нет, есть, and prepositions across all three genders. Identify the trigger, apply the form.

title: Genitive: Exceptions & Edge Cases
description: The standard genitive rule covers most nouns, but three families slip through: 3rd-declension feminines, -мя neuters, and meaning-overrides-ending masculines. This lesson teaches them.

title: Negation 1: The Particle не
description: Russian builds its everyday negation around one short word: не. Today we learn where to place it (right before the negated element) and the four kinds of element it can negate: verb, noun, adjective, and adverb.

title: Negation 2: Нет + Genitive
description: When Russian wants to say something does not exist, has not arrived, or is missing, it uses нет followed by the noun in the genitive. Three frames cover almost every A1 use: bare absence, possession, and absence at a location.

title: Negation 3: Negative Pronouns and the Double Negative
titleEnglish: Negation 3: Negative Pronouns and the Double Negative
description: Russian has a family of ни-words (никто, ничего, никогда, нигде, никуда, никак) for 'nobody / nothing / never / nowhere / no way.' Every ни-word demands a не on the verb. The result is the Russian double negative, which sounds strange in English but is mandatory here.

title: Negation 4: Ни...ни... and Emphatic Ни
description: Russian uses the particle ни to coordinate two negated items ('neither bread nor milk') and to add emphasis to a noun in a negated sentence ('not a single word'). Both uses keep the not-yet-familiar but mandatory не on the verb.

title: Negation 5: Mixed Review
description: Russian A1 negation runs on four moves: не on a target, нет + genitive for absence, ни-words paired with не on the verb, and ни...ни... / ни одного for coordinated and emphatic negation. Today we mix them and learn to name which move is operating.

title: Nouns 1: The Base Form and Three Genders
titleEnglish: Nouns 1: The Base Form and Three Genders
description: Every Russian noun has a fixed gender, and you can almost always read it straight off the last letter of the dictionary form (the nominative). Hard consonant signals masculine; -а or -я signals feminine; -о or -е signals neuter.

title: Nouns 2: The Soft Sign and the Tricky Ones
titleEnglish: Nouns 2: The Soft Sign and the Tricky Ones
description: The basic ending rule from lesson 1 covers most Russian nouns, but it leaves three small gaps: soft-sign -ь nouns (which can go either way), nouns whose meaning overrides their ending (папа is masculine), and a tiny closed set of -мя neuters (время, имя). This lesson trains all three.

title: Nouns 3: Making Plurals with -ы and -и
description: Most Russian plurals are formed by swapping the singular ending for -ы or -и. The choice between them is governed by a small but powerful orthographic rule (the seven-letter rule): after Г, К, Х and Ж, Ш, Щ, Ч, Russian never writes -ы; it always writes -и.

title: Nouns 4: Making Plurals with -а and -я
description: Two groups of Russian nouns form their plurals with -а or -я instead of -ы / -и. Neuters are regular: -о → -а, -е → -я (окно → окна, море → моря). A small set of masculines is irregular and high-frequency: дом → дома, город → города, профессор → профессора, учитель → учителя.

title: Nouns 5: Quirky Plurals and Always / Never Plural
titleEnglish: Nouns 5: Quirky Plurals and Always / Never Plural
description: Three small sets of Russian nouns refuse to follow the regular plural rules: truly irregular plurals (друг → друзья, ребёнок → дети, мать → матери), nouns that exist only in the plural (часы, очки, деньги), and nouns that exist only in the singular (молоко, мясо). All three sets are short, closed, and full of everyday words.

title: Nouns 6: Mixed Review (Naming the World)
description: Mixed review of the whole track. Read gender from the ending (with the soft-sign and male-person patches). Form the plural, with the seven-letter rule, the irregular -а / -я set, the truly irregular forms, and the plural-only / singular-only nouns. One system, the right form every time.

title: Numbers 1: Counting from One to Ten
titleEnglish: Numbers 1: Counting from One to Ten
description: Meet the first ten Russian numbers as words. Today is pronunciation, recognition, and ordering. No grammar rules, no noun endings - just the sounds and shapes of один, два, три through десять.

title: Numbers 2: One Agrees (один, одна, одно)
description: Russian's number one is the only cardinal that matches its noun. Today we lock the three main forms: один (m), одна (f), одно (n). The plural form одни waits for Lesson 3.

title: Numbers 3: One Pair (одни with plural-only nouns)
titleEnglish: Numbers 3: One Pair (одни with plural-only nouns)
description: A small group of Russian nouns has no singular form: часы (watch), джинсы (jeans), очки (glasses), ножницы (scissors). With these, 'one' takes a fourth form: одни. A short, focused lesson on this single use.

title: Numbers 4: Meet 'Two' (два and две, masculine and feminine)
titleEnglish: Numbers 4: Meet 'Two' (два and две, masculine and feminine)
description: The number two does something new: it reshapes the noun. Два брата, две сестры. Today we focus on just the masculine and feminine versions, with one ending change to learn at a time.

title: Numbers 5: Two of These, Two of Those (два with neuter nouns)
titleEnglish: Numbers 5: Two of These, Two of Those (два with neuter nouns)
description: We extend yesterday's two rule to neuter nouns. Два окна, два письма, два моря. Same rule as masculine: the noun gains an -а in the genitive singular. A short, focused lesson that fills the last gender slot for two.

title: Numbers 6: Three and Four (same rule, no gender)
titleEnglish: Numbers 6: Three and Four (same rule, no gender)
description: Three and four follow the exact rule you learned for two: they reshape the noun into the genitive singular. The relief is that три and четыре have no gender forms - one shape covers every noun.

title: Numbers 7: Five to Ten (a new form on the noun)
titleEnglish: Numbers 7: Five to Ten (a new form on the noun)
description: From five onward, the rule changes again. Пять, шесть, семь, восемь, девять, десять take a different form on the noun: the genitive plural. Today we cover the two cleanest endings: -ов for masculine consonants and the zero ending for feminine -а.

title: Numbers 8: The Teens (11-19 always take the genitive plural)
titleEnglish: Numbers 8: The Teens (11-19 always take the genitive plural)
description: Meet the teen words одиннадцать through девятнадцать. They all share one rule: the noun goes into the genitive plural, just as it did after five. The second digit does not matter - twelve behaves like fifteen, not like two.

title: Numbers 9: Round Tens and a Hundred (20, 30, 40, 50, 100)
titleEnglish: Numbers 9: Round Tens and a Hundred (20, 30, 40, 50, 100)
description: Meet двадцать, тридцать, сорок, пятьдесят, шестьдесят, семьдесят, восемьдесят, девяносто, сто. The round tens and one hundred all act like the numbers from five upward: the noun goes into the genitive plural.

title: Numbers 10: How Old Are You? (год, года, лет)
titleEnglish: Numbers 10: How Old Are You? (год, года, лет)
description: All nine previous lessons brought to one daily question: how old are you? The word for 'year' has three forms - год, года, лет - and which one you use depends on the same rules you have been building. This is the synthesis lesson.

title: Possessives 1: Mine and Yours (мой / твой)
description: Russian possessive pronouns agree with the noun they describe, just like adjectives. Today we drill the four forms of мой and твой across masculine, feminine, neuter, and plural.

title: Possessives 2: Ours and Yours (наш / ваш)
description: The 'our' and 'your-plural-or-polite' possessives follow the same four-form pattern as мой and твой. Today we drill наш / наша / наше / наши and ваш / ваша / ваше / ваши.

title: Possessives 3: His, Her, Their (Invariant)
description: The trio его / её / их never change shape. Unlike мой and наш, these three forms ignore the gender and number of the noun completely. This is the highest-failure-rate possessive rule at A1.

title: Possessives 4: This and That (этот / тот)
description: Demonstrative pronouns этот, эта, это, эти ('this / these') and тот, та, то, те ('that / those') agree with the noun, like мой and наш. Today we drill the four forms of each.

title: Possessives 5: Chains (этот + мой + adjective + noun)
description: Russian lets you stack a demonstrative, a possessive, and an adjective in front of one noun. Each layer agrees with the noun in gender and number. Today we drill the full chain.

title: Possessives 6: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis of all five lessons. The possessives мой / твой and наш / ваш, the invariant trio (его / её / их), demonstratives (этот / тот), and full agreement chains.

title: Prepositional 1: Where? (After 'в')
description: After 'в' (in/at), the noun shifts into the prepositional case. Most nouns take -е; nouns ending in -ия (Россия) take -ии.

title: Prepositional 2: After 'на'
description: After 'на' (on/at), the noun shifts to the prepositional case. Same forms as after 'в.' Today also introduces feminine -я → -е.

title: Prepositional 3: 'в' or 'на'?
description: The case form is the same after в and на. The choice depends on the noun's category. Drill the decision.

title: Prepositional 4: 'о' (About)
description: After 'о' (about), the noun shifts into the prepositional case. Same form rules as for в and на.

title: Prepositional 5: 'о' or 'об'?
description: 'О' becomes 'об' before vowel-initial nouns. There is also a rare 'обо' variant.

title: Prepositional 6: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis. Mixes в, на, о, об across all genders, including the -ия → -ии pattern from L1.

title: Prepositional: Exceptions & Edge Cases
description: Beyond the -е rule: the stressed locative -у/-ю (в лесу́, на полу́), soft-sign masculines and 3rd-declension feminines (о словаре, о матери), and the idiomatic на-collocations (на работе, на почте).

title: Present Tense 1: First Conjugation Core
description: Russian splits its verbs into two big conjugation classes. Today we drill the first one: the -ю / -ешь / -ет / -ем / -ете / -ют endings on the cleanest verbs in the language.

title: Present Tense 2: Second Conjugation Core
description: The other big conjugation class. Most -ить verbs (and some -еть, -ать) take a different ending set: -ю / -ишь / -ит / -им / -ите / -ят.

title: Present Tense 3: Stress Shifts
description: Many Russian verbs put the stress on the ending in the я-form, then shift it back onto the stem for ты, он, мы, вы, они. Today we lock that pattern.

title: Present Tense 4: 1sg Consonant Mutations
description: Many 2nd-conjugation verbs change a consonant in the я-form only. Любить → люблю, видеть → вижу, готовить → готовлю. The rest of the paradigm uses the unmutated stem.

title: Present Tense 5: Husher Spelling Rule
description: After the hushers ж, ш, ч, щ, Russian writes -у and -а instead of -ю and -я. So учить → учу (not 'учю') and учат (not 'учят'). Today we lock that.

title: Present Tense 6: Core Irregulars (хотеть, мочь, есть)
titleEnglish: Present Tense 6: Core Irregulars (хотеть, мочь, есть)
description: Three of the most-used Russian verbs do their own thing. Хотеть mixes both conjugations. Мочь alternates between two stems. Есть has its own tiny paradigm.

title: Present Tense 7: More Core Irregulars
description: Five more high-frequency irregulars. Жить, пить, петь have unusual stems. Идти and ехать are the unidirectional motion verbs every A1 learner needs from week one.

title: Present Tense 8: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis. Mixed quiz across all seven prior rules: 1st and 2nd conjugation, stress shifts, 1sg mutations, the husher rule, and the high-frequency irregulars.

title: Adjective Declension 1: Foundation and the Four Nominative Slots
titleEnglish: Adjective Declension 1: Foundation and the Four Nominative Slots
description: Restart point for adjective work at A2: the four nominative endings (-ый / -ая / -ое / -ые) locked one more time, with a short preview of what each oblique case will do to those endings later in the track.

title: Adjective Declension 2: Accusative Singular and the Animacy Split
titleEnglish: Adjective Declension 2: Accusative Singular and the Animacy Split
description: The accusative singular for hard-stem adjectives. The masculine inanimate keeps the nominative form (-ый). The masculine animate borrows the genitive form (-ого). The feminine has its own ending (-ую). The neuter is always like the nominative (-ое).

title: Adjective Declension 3: Genitive Singular
description: The genitive singular for hard-stem adjectives. The masculine and neuter share -ого. The feminine has -ой. The same endings cover possession (у меня нет ...), absence, and the prepositions из / у / без / для / от.

title: Adjective Declension 4: Dative Singular
description: The dative singular for hard-stem adjectives. Masculine and neuter share -ому. The feminine reuses -ой (the same form as the genitive). Triggers: помогать, звонить, дать, нравиться, рад, the preposition к, age, and the impersonal 'мне холодно' family.

title: Adjective Declension 5: Instrumental Singular
description: The instrumental singular for hard-stem adjectives. Masculine and neuter share -ым (with husher / velar -им). Feminine reuses -ой. Triggers: с + accompaniment, instrumental of profession (работать кем), means of transport, the prepositions с / за / под / над / перед.

title: Adjective Declension 6: Prepositional Singular
description: The prepositional singular for hard-stem adjectives. Masculine and neuter share -ом. The feminine reuses -ой. Triggers: в, на, о / об, при + prepositional. The prepositional always sits behind a preposition.

title: Adjective Declension 7: Plural Across All Six Cases
titleEnglish: Adjective Declension 7: Plural Across All Six Cases
description: The plural across the full six-case paradigm. Russian collapses gender in the plural for adjectives: one ending per case, no masc / fem / neut split. The animacy split returns in the plural accusative.

title: Adjective Declension 8: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis. All six cases × singular and plural × the husher / velar spelling rule. The four-step diagnostic (gender / number → case → spelling rule → ending) runs the full grid.

title: Adjective Declension: Exceptions & Edge Cases
description: The eight-lesson core taught the hard-stem grid (with the husher / velar wrinkle). This lesson teaches the two parallel paradigms that sit outside it: soft-stem adjectives in -ний (синий, последний, домашний, осенний) and the possessive-style adjectives in -ин / -ов (мамин, папин, отцов).

title: Aspect 1: Process vs Completion
description: Russian verbs come in pairs. The imperfective focuses on the process; the perfective focuses on completion. Today: recognizing the difference.

title: Aspect 2: Recognizing Aspect Pairs
description: Aspect pairs follow predictable form patterns. Today: prefix-added pairs, suffix-change pairs, and a few suppletive (different-root) pairs.

title: Aspect 3: Aspect in the Past Tense
titleEnglish: Aspect 3: Aspect in the Past Tense
description: The past tense is where aspect choice matters most. Today: drilling imperfective vs perfective past with gender and number agreement.

title: Aspect 4: Duration and Habit Trigger Imperfective
titleEnglish: Aspect 4: Duration and Habit Trigger Imperfective
description: Time markers that describe duration (весь день, два часа, долго) or habit (часто, каждый день, обычно) trigger the imperfective.

title: Aspect 5: Result and Completion Trigger Perfective
titleEnglish: Aspect 5: Result and Completion Trigger Perfective
description: Time markers that signal completion (уже, наконец, за час, к утру) trigger the perfective. Today: identifying these cues and choosing the perfective past.

title: Aspect 6: Future Tense (Two Futures)
description: Russian has two futures, one for each aspect. Imperfective: буду + infinitive. Perfective: present-tense conjugation of the perfective verb.

title: Aspect 7: Mixed Review (All Triggers, Both Tenses)
titleEnglish: Aspect 7: Mixed Review (All Triggers, Both Tenses)
description: Synthesis. Mixes process vs completion, duration vs result, and the two futures.

title: Comparatives 1: The One-Word Form (stem + ее)
description: Russian builds 'newer, prettier, more interesting' by adding -ее to the adjective stem. The result is one word that never changes for gender or number.

title: Comparatives 2: The Four You Must Memorise (лучше, хуже, больше, меньше)
titleEnglish: Comparatives 2: The Four You Must Memorise (лучше, хуже, больше, меньше)
description: Four of the most common Russian comparatives are completely irregular and cannot be built by rule: хороший → лучше, плохой → хуже, большой → больше, маленький → меньше. Learn them as fixed words.

title: Comparatives 3: When the Last Consonant Changes
titleEnglish: Comparatives 3: When the Last Consonant Changes
description: Six common comparatives swap their last consonant and end in -е: дороже (more expensive), тише (quieter), проще (simpler), ближе (closer), легче (easier), моложе (younger). Today you learn to spot and build these six.

title: Comparatives 4: Short Forms (выше, ниже, дальше, дешевле, старше, шире)
titleEnglish: Comparatives 4: Short Forms (выше, ниже, дальше, дешевле, старше, шире)
description: Six very common comparatives drop part of their adjective and become short one-word forms: высокий → выше, низкий → ниже, далёкий → дальше, дешёвый → дешевле, старый → старше, широкий → шире. Today you learn to recognise and use these six.

title: Comparatives 5: Two Ways to Say "Than"
description: Russian has two equally correct ways to say 'than': чем + nominative (старше, чем брат) or the bare genitive with no preposition (старше брата). A pronoun or a whole clause forces чем; a short noun usually prefers the bare genitive.

title: Comparatives 6: Twice as Big (в + раз)
description: To say 'twice as X' or 'three times as X' in Russian, use 'в + a number in the accusative + раз / раза + a comparative': в два раза больше, в три раза дороже.

title: Comparatives 7: более + Adjective Before a Noun
titleEnglish: Comparatives 7: более + Adjective Before a Noun
description: To say 'a more X thing' before a noun, put более ('more') in front of a normal adjective. Более never changes; the adjective changes its ending to match the noun.

title: Comparatives 8: Saying "Less" with менее
description: Менее ('less') sits before an ordinary adjective to make a comparative in the opposite direction. The adjective agrees with its noun; менее never changes. Some adjectives, like -ский words, only build the comparative this way.

title: Comparatives 9: The Most X (самый + adjective)
description: The everyday way to say 'the most X / the X-est' is самый + adjective. Both words agree with the noun in gender, number, and case. Add из + genitive plural to say 'of all,' and use лучший / худший for 'best / worst.'

title: Comparatives 10: Mixed Review (all forms together)
description: The finisher for the track. Every comparative and superlative form meets in one place: the regular -ее, the irregular -е, the чем and bare-genitive 'than', the compound более / менее, and the superlative самый. You spot which form is at work and pick the right one. No new grammar.

title: Conjunctions 1: и vs а (Adding vs Contrasting)
titleEnglish: Conjunctions 1: и vs а (Adding vs Contrasting)
description: English and covers two different Russian words. И adds two ideas going the same way (Я учусь и работаю). А sets up a parallel contrast (Я учусь, а он работает). When the halves are parallel but differ, Russian almost always wants а.

title: Conjunctions 2: но (Real Contrast, Broken Expectation)
description: Но is the strong but: it signals that the second half breaks the expectation set by the first. Я учился, но не сдал. If English however fits, Russian wants но - not а.

title: Conjunctions 3: потому что vs поэтому (Why vs So)
titleEnglish: Conjunctions 3: потому что vs поэтому (Why vs So)
description: Потому что answers why (the reason follows). Поэтому states the result (the consequence follows). They point in opposite directions: Он остался дома, потому что был болен. Он был болен, поэтому остался дома.

title: Conjunctions 4: тоже vs также (Me Too vs And Also This)
titleEnglish: Conjunctions 4: тоже vs также (Me Too vs And Also This)
description: Тоже adds the same comment to a NEW subject (Антон тоже прочитал её). Также adds a NEW fact about the SAME subject (Я также написал отзыв). One does 'me too'; the other does 'and also this'.

title: Conjunctions 5: Mixed Review (и, а, но, потому что, поэтому, тоже, также)
titleEnglish: Conjunctions 5: Mixed Review (и, а, но, потому что, поэтому, тоже, также)
description: Pull the whole track together: in one mixed set, pick the conjunction that fits - simple addition (и), parallel contrast (а), broken expectation (но), cause (потому что), result (поэтому), or one of the two also words (тоже / также).

title: Dative 1: To Whom? (All Three Genders)
description: The dative case answers 'Кому?' (To whom?). Today: singular dative endings for masculine, feminine, and neuter nouns.

title: Dative 2: Giving and Sending (Verbs of Transfer)
titleEnglish: Dative 2: Giving and Sending (Verbs of Transfer)
description: Verbs of giving and transferring (давать, дарить, покупать, писать, посылать) take a dative recipient. Drill the recipient form across genders.

title: Dative 3: 'I Like It' (Нравится)
description: The 'нравится' construction puts the LIKER in the dative and the LIKED THING in the nominative. Today drills the dative personal pronouns and verb agreement.

title: Dative 4: Age (Маше двадцать лет)
description: Russian expresses age with the dative case: 'Маше двадцать лет.' The person whose age is being given goes in the dative.

title: Dative 5: Feelings and States (Мне холодно)
description: Russian uses the dative for feelings and physical states: 'Мне холодно' (I'm cold), 'Маше весело' (Masha is having fun). The experiencer is dative.

title: Dative 6: Motion Toward (к + dative)
description: The preposition к (toward) takes the dative case. Used with motion verbs: 'Я иду к маме' (I'm going to mom).

title: Dative 7: Mixed Review (All Triggers, All Genders)
titleEnglish: Dative 7: Mixed Review (All Triggers, All Genders)
description: Synthesis lesson. Mixes verbs of giving, нравится, age, feelings, and к + motion across all genders.

title: Dative: Exceptions & Edge Cases
description: The dative-form exceptions that sit outside the seven regular lessons: 3rd-declension feminine nouns ending in -ь (мать → ма́тери, дочь → до́чери, тетра́дь → тетра́ди) with the мать / дочь stem extension, the -мя neuters (вре́мя → вре́мени, и́мя → и́мени), and the small set of plurale-tantum dative forms (часа́м, деньга́м, очка́м) at recognition level.

title: Future Tense 1: Буду - the Future of Быть
titleEnglish: Future Tense 1: Буду - the Future of Быть
description: The six future forms of быть: буду / будешь / будет / будем / будете / будут. Saying where you will be, what there will be, and what the weather will be like.

title: Future Tense 5: Plans, Promises, and Time Words
titleEnglish: Future Tense 5: Plans, Promises, and Time Words
description: The future tense in real life: making plans, promising, and the time words that anchor them - завтра, через час, на следующей неделе, скоро, потом.

title: Future Tense 6: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis of the whole future tense: the future of быть, the two-word imperfective future, the one-word perfective future, choosing between them, and the future time words.

title: Imperative 1: Vowel-Stem Commands (читай, делай, открой)
description: How to give a command to one person (ты) for verbs whose они-form ends in -ют: read the они-form, drop the ending, add -й. читать → читай, делать → делай, открыть → открой, играть → играй.

title: Imperative 2: Consonant Stem + Stressed -и (говори, пиши)
description: When the verb stem ends in a consonant and the я-form ending is stressed (говорю́, пишу́, иду́, куплю́), the 2sg command adds -и: говори, пиши, иди, купи.

title: Imperative 3: The -ь Command and the Stress Test (-и or -ь)
titleEnglish: Imperative 3: The -ь Command and the Stress Test (-и or -ь)
description: How to choose between -и and -ь on a consonant-stem command: stressed 1sg ending gives -и (говори), unstressed gives -ь (готовь, забудь, встань). A few cluster and irregular forms (помни, ешь, дай) are exceptions.

title: Imperative 4: Plural and Polite Forms (add -те)
description: Add -те to the 2sg command to address two or more people OR one person politely (вы): читай → читайте, говори → говорите, готовь → готовьте. The suffix -й / -и / -ь does not change.

title: Imperative 5: Habit vs One Result (читай каждый день / прочитай эту статью)
titleEnglish: Imperative 5: Habit vs One Result (читай каждый день / прочитай эту статью)
description: A command can be imperfective or perfective. Use the imperfective (читай каждый день) for a habit or process, and the perfective (прочитай эту статью) for one specific action you want finished.

title: Imperative 6: Saying "Don't" (не + Imperfective)
description: A general prohibition uses не plus the imperfective imperative: не пей, не кури, не говори громко. The negative flips the affirmative perfective default.

title: Imperative 7: "Careful!" Warnings (не + Perfective)
description: Не + perfective is the warning form: не забудь, не упади, не опоздай, не разбей. It warns against one accidental, unwanted result. The general prohibition не + imperfective is the opposite, and today's drills make you tell them apart.

title: Imperative 8: "Let's" Suggestions and Polite Requests
description: Make 'let's' suggestions with давай / давайте (+ imperfective infinitive for a process, + 1pl perfective future for one action), and soften a command into a request with пожалуйста, будьте добры, or если можно.

title: Imperative 9: Mixed Review (Name the Step)
description: The finisher for the Imperative track. Everything from formation and aspect to negation, давай / давайте, and softeners comes back together. The main skill today is naming which step decided each form.

title: Instrumental 1: With What? (Masculine)
description: The instrumental case answers 'Кем? Чем?' (By whom? With what?). Today: masculine singular endings -ом and -ем.

title: Instrumental 2: Feminine -ой / -ей
description: Feminine instrumental endings: -а → -ой, -я → -ей. Drilled with пишет ручкой, интересуется музыкой, гордится тётей.

title: Instrumental 3: С + Instrumental (With)
description: The preposition с (with) takes the instrumental for accompaniment. Today: с другом, с мамой, с молоком, plus neuter -о → -ом.

title: Instrumental 4: Professions and Identities
description: Professions take instrumental after работать, быть (past / future), and стать. Я работаю инженером.

title: Instrumental 5: Means of Transport
description: Russian expresses 'by bus / by car' two ways: 'на + prepositional' (everyday speech) and the bare instrumental (more formal). Today drills the conversational form with the bare instrumental as the formal alternative.

title: Instrumental 6: За, Под, Над, Перед (Position)
description: Position prepositions за / под / над / перед take the instrumental for STATIC location: за столом, под стулом, над окном.

title: Instrumental 7: 3rd-Declension Feminine and Adverbial Use
description: Feminine nouns ending in soft -ь (дверь, ночь, площадь) take -ью in the instrumental. The bare instrumental of time-of-day and season nouns also serves as adverbs: ночью (at night), утром (in the morning), летом (in summer).

title: Instrumental 8: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis of all seven instrumental contexts: tool / means, reflexive verbs, с (with), professions, transport, position prepositions, and 3rd-declension feminine + adverbial use.

title: Instrumental: Exceptions & Edge Cases
description: The forms that fall outside the regular -ом / -ой / -ью pattern: the мать / дочь stem extension drilled in production, instrumental of plural-only nouns (часами, ножницами, сутками, деньгами), frozen adverbial instrumentals beyond time-of-day (бегом, шагом, рядом, пешком), and a brief look at the instrumental of small numerals (двумя, тремя, четырьмя).

title: Necessity 1: Мне надо (the dative subject)
description: To say 'I have to' in Russian, the person goes into the DATIVE: Мне надо... / Мне нужно..., not 'я надо.' Надо and нужно are impersonal and never agree with anyone.

title: Necessity 2: должен / должна / должны (agreement)
description: Должен ('must, obliged') is personal: the subject stays NOMINATIVE and должен agrees with it in gender and number (должен / должна / должно / должны), plus an infinitive.

title: Necessity 3: нельзя and можно (forbidden, impossible, allowed)
titleEnglish: Necessity 3: нельзя and можно (forbidden, impossible, allowed)
description: Можно means 'one may.' Нельзя is its opposite, but its meaning depends on aspect: нельзя + imperfective = forbidden; нельзя + perfective = impossible.

title: Necessity 4: Past and Future (надо было, надо будет, должен был)
titleEnglish: Necessity 4: Past and Future (надо было, надо будет, должен был)
description: Add было for past necessity and будет for future. With надо/нужно the copula stays neuter (надо было). With должен it agrees with the subject (должен был / должна была).

title: Necessity 5: The Strength Spectrum (можно / стоит / нужно / придётся)
titleEnglish: Necessity 5: The Strength Spectrum (можно / стоит / нужно / придётся)
description: Necessity comes in degrees. From soft to hard: можно (may) - стоит (worth doing) - нужно/надо (need to) - придётся (will have to, unavoidable). Придётся takes the dative and usually a perfective infinitive.

title: Necessity 6: Putting It All Together
description: A mixed review of the whole track: надо/нужно (dative), должен (nominative, agrees), нельзя/можно with aspect, past and future, and the can/should/must/will-have-to spectrum.

title: Past Tense 2: Был, Была, Было, Были
titleEnglish: Past Tense 2: Был, Была, Было, Были
description: The past of быть (to be): был / была / было / были. Saying where someone was, what there was, and what the weather was like.

title: Past Tense 3: Tricky Agreement
description: Agreement practice on the tricky subjects: polite вы, masculine -а nouns like папа and дедушка, the question word кто, and compound subjects like Антон и Лена.

title: Past Tense 5: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis of the whole past tense: regular formation, быть, tricky agreement, the irregular -чь / -ти families, and stress shifts. Four-step diagnostic: subject → family → ending → stress.

title: Pronoun Declension 1: Personal Pronouns in the Accusative and Genitive
titleEnglish: Pronoun Declension 1: Personal Pronouns in the Accusative and Genitive
description: The seven personal pronouns (я, ты, он, она, мы, вы, они) and their accusative / genitive forms (меня, тебя, его, её, нас, вас, их). For personal pronouns the accusative and genitive are identical, because every speaker and listener is animate.

title: Pronoun Declension 2: Personal Pronouns in the Dative, Instrumental, and Prepositional
titleEnglish: Pronoun Declension 2: Personal Pronouns in the Dative, Instrumental, and Prepositional
description: The remaining three cases for the seven personal pronouns. Dative: мне, тебе, ему, ей, нам, вам, им. Instrumental: мной, тобой, им, ей, нами, вами, ими. Prepositional: обо мне, о тебе, о нём, о ней, о нас, о вас, о них.

title: Pronoun Declension 3: The н- Prefix on 3rd-Person Pronouns After Prepositions
titleEnglish: Pronoun Declension 3: The н- Prefix on 3rd-Person Pronouns After Prepositions
description: After a preposition, the 3rd-person pronouns (он, она, оно, они) gain a leading н-: его → у него, ей → к ней, их → с ними. The 1st and 2nd person never take this prefix. Highest-failure-rate A2 pronoun rule.

title: Pronoun Declension 4: Possessive Declension Across All Six Cases
titleEnglish: Pronoun Declension 4: Possessive Declension Across All Six Cases
description: The possessives мой, твой, наш, ваш decline like adjectives across the six cases: моего, моему, моим, о моём; моей; моих, моими, о моих. The invariant trio его / её / их never agrees and never declines.

title: Pronoun Declension 5: Demonstratives Across All Six Cases (этот, тот, чей)
titleEnglish: Pronoun Declension 5: Demonstratives Across All Six Cases (этот, тот, чей)
description: Этот / тот decline across all six cases like adjectives, with their own irregular instrumental masc / neut form (этим, тем, not 'этом'). Чей (whose) declines on the same pattern as the soft possessive мой.

title: Pronoun Declension 6: Mixed Review and the Reflexive Pronoun себя
titleEnglish: Pronoun Declension 6: Mixed Review and the Reflexive Pronoun себя
description: Synthesis of the five lessons in this track plus the reflexive pronoun себя (oneself), which has no nominative and uses one form across the acc / gen, separate forms for dat (себе), instr (собой), and prep (о себе).

title: Reflexive 1: Choosing -ся or -сь
description: Some Russian verbs end in -ся or -сь. The choice is about sound: -сь follows a vowel, -ся follows a consonant or soft sign. Today we drill that one choice across the present and past tenses.

title: Reflexive 2: Wash Yourself vs Wash Something
titleEnglish: Reflexive 2: Wash Yourself vs Wash Something
description: Use the reflexive verb (мыться, одеваться, бриться, причёсываться) when the action goes back to the subject. Use the plain twin (мыть, одевать) when there is a separate object being acted on.

title: Reflexive 3: Getting Ready (готовиться к, собираться, купаться)
titleEnglish: Reflexive 3: Getting Ready (готовиться к, собираться, купаться)
description: Three everyday reflexive verbs of getting ready: готовиться к + dative (prepare for), собираться + infinitive (be about to), and купаться (bathe, swim). Each keeps the -ся / -сь ending; готовиться needs the dative after к, and собираться links straight to an infinitive.

title: Reflexive 4: Each Other (plural subject)
description: Some -ся verbs describe a mutual action: people do it to each other. With a plural subject (Они обнимаются), one verb covers everyone, and no partner phrase is needed.

title: Reflexive 5: Naming the Partner (с / со + instrumental)
titleEnglish: Reflexive 5: Naming the Partner (с / со + instrumental)
description: Reciprocal reflexives like встречаться, знакомиться and переписываться name the other person with с + the instrumental case: с Антоном, с сестрой. Use со instead of с before a hard cluster of consonants.

title: Reflexive 6: Liking (нравиться + dative)
description: To say someone likes something, Russian uses нравиться. The person who likes goes in the dative, and the thing they like is the nominative subject. The verb agrees with that thing.

title: Reflexive 7: Being Afraid (+ genitive)
description: Бояться (to be afraid of) and стесняться (to be shy of) name the source of the feeling in the genitive, not the accusative. Антон боится темноты, not темноту.

title: Reflexive 8: Activities and Interests (+ instrumental)
description: Four common -ся verbs take the instrumental case for their object: заниматься (do an activity), интересоваться (be interested in), гордиться (be proud of), пользоваться (use). Today you practise putting that object in the instrumental.

title: Reflexive 9: смеяться над, надеяться на, стараться + verb
titleEnglish: Reflexive 9: смеяться над, надеяться на, стараться + verb
description: Three fixed frames to memorise as units: смеяться над + instrumental (laugh at), надеяться на + accusative (hope for), and стараться / учиться + infinitive (try / learn to do).

title: Reflexive 10: The Passive Use (дом строится)
description: The -ся marker can make a sentence passive: the subject is the thing that the action happens to. Дом строится means 'The house is being built.' If you name who does it, that doer goes in the instrumental: строится рабочими.

title: Reflexive 11: It Starts on Its Own (начинаться)
titleEnglish: Reflexive 11: It Starts on Its Own (начинаться)
description: Many verbs have a -ся twin with no doer. Начинать урок (begin the lesson) versus Урок начинается (the lesson begins). The thing that was the object becomes the subject, and nobody is named as doing it.

title: Reflexive 12: Mixed Review (What Job Is -ся Doing?)
titleEnglish: Reflexive 12: Mixed Review (What Job Is -ся Doing?)
description: The finisher for the whole track. The ending -ся / -сь does five different jobs. Today you name the job in any sentence and produce the right form. Nothing new is taught.

title: Past Tense 1: Regular Formation
description: The regular past tense in Russian. Drop the -ть of the infinitive and add -л / -ла / -ло / -ли. The form agrees with the SUBJECT in gender and number, not with the speaker.

title: Past Tense 4: Irregular Past Tense
description: Irregular past forms with no -л in the masculine: the -чь class (мог, лёг, пёк) and the -ти / -сти class (шёл, нёс, вёл). The feminine, neuter, and plural still take regular -ла / -ло / -ли endings.

title: Future Tense 2: Imperfective Future (буду + infinitive)
description: The imperfective future tense in Russian: буду / будешь / будет / будем / будете / будут + the imperfective infinitive. Two-word future for processes, habits, and ongoing actions.

title: Future Tense 3: Perfective Future (One Word)
description: The perfective future tense in Russian. The same conjugation as the present tense, but applied to a perfective verb. Single-word future for completed, bounded actions: я прочитаю, я скажу, я напишу.

title: Future Tense 4: Process or Result - Choosing Your Future
titleEnglish: Future Tense 4: Process or Result - Choosing Your Future
description: Choosing between the two futures: буду читать for ongoing or habitual action, прочитаю for one bounded result. The same choice viewed in the past tense for contrast.

title: Time 1: Который час? (час / часа / часов)
description: To say what o'clock it is, count the hours: один час, два часа, пять часов. The word for 'hour' changes with the number: 1 takes час, 2-4 take часа, 5 and up take часов. This is the core numeral-agreement rule, met first on the clock.

title: Time 2: в понедельник (on a day, at a time)
titleEnglish: Time 2: в понедельник (on a day, at a time)
description: To say something happens ON a day or AT a clock time, use в + accusative: в понедельник (on Monday), в среду (on Wednesday), в два часа (at two o'clock). For most days the accusative looks like the dictionary form; feminine -а days change to -у (среда → среду).

title: Time 3: первого мая (dates and months)
description: To give a date, put the day as an ordinal number in the genitive and the month in the genitive: первого мая (the first of May), пятого марта (the fifth of March). The same phrase answers both 'what date is it' and 'on what date.' Years use a long ordinal in the prepositional: в две тысячи двадцать пятом году.

title: Time 4: через час, час назад (in / ago)
titleEnglish: Time 4: через час, час назад (in / ago)
description: To say something happens IN / AFTER a stretch of time, use через + accusative BEFORE the phrase: через час (in an hour). To say AGO, put the time in the accusative and add назад AFTER it: час назад (an hour ago). Через comes before; назад comes after.

title: Time 5: по понедельникам, утром (how often, when of day)
titleEnglish: Time 5: по понедельникам, утром (how often, when of day)
description: For something that repeats on certain days, use по + dative plural: по понедельникам (on Mondays). For the parts of the day use NO preposition - just the instrumental: утром, днём, вечером, ночью. 'Every day' is каждый день in the accusative.

title: Time 6: Mixed Review (pin any event in time)
titleEnglish: Time 6: Mixed Review (pin any event in time)
description: Bring the whole track together: Который час and час/часа/часов; в + accusative for clock times and days; the genitive for dates; через ... and ... назад; по + dative for recurring days and the bare instrumental for parts of the day. Choose the right preposition and case for each kind of time phrase.

title: Aspect Deep 1: Aspect in Negation
description: Negation changes the aspect calculus. Не + imperfective: the action did not take place at all. Не + perfective: the action took place but did not reach completion.

title: Aspect Deep 2: Frequency Adverbs and Habitual Patterns
titleEnglish: Aspect Deep 2: Frequency Adverbs and Habitual Patterns
description: Beyond часто and всегда. The B1 frequency family adds редко, никогда, постоянно, регулярно, and habitual time patterns like по утрам and по выходным.

title: Aspect Deep 3: Completion and Sudden-Event Adverbs
titleEnglish: Aspect Deep 3: Completion and Sudden-Event Adverbs
description: Beyond уже and наконец. The B1 completion family adds наконец-то, мгновенно, вдруг, неожиданно, and the 'успеть + СВ' construction. All push you toward the perfective.

title: Aspect Deep 4: Aspect in the Imperative
titleEnglish: Aspect Deep 4: Aspect in the Imperative
description: Imperatives carry aspect. Pf imperative for one specific request (Прочитай!), impf for habitual or process commands (Читай!). Negative pf for warnings against accidents (Не разбей!).

title: Aspect Deep 5: Phase Verbs Take Imperfective Infinitives
titleEnglish: Aspect Deep 5: Phase Verbs Take Imperfective Infinitives
description: Verbs that mark the start, continuation, or end of an action (начать, продолжать, закончить, перестать, бросить, стать) take ONLY an imperfective infinitive.

title: Aspect Deep 6: Хотеть, Любить, Мочь and the Infinitive
titleEnglish: Aspect Deep 6: Хотеть, Любить, Мочь and the Infinitive
description: Verbs of desire, preference, and ability default to imperfective infinitives. The perfective appears when there is a specific bounded result in mind.

title: Aspect Deep 7: Aspect in the Conditional
titleEnglish: Aspect Deep 7: Aspect in the Conditional
description: The conditional is built from past-tense forms with бы. Aspect choice in if-clauses and result-clauses follows the same rules as in the plain past.

title: Aspect Deep 8: Sequencing and Background in Narration
titleEnglish: Aspect Deep 8: Sequencing and Background in Narration
description: How aspect builds a narrative. Chained perfectives carry the storyline; the imperfective provides the background against which perfective events happen.

title: Aspect Deep 9: Mixed Review (All Eight Contexts)
titleEnglish: Aspect Deep 9: Mixed Review (All Eight Contexts)
description: Synthesis. Mixes negation, frequency, completion, imperatives, phase verbs, modal verbs, the conditional, and narrative sequencing.

title: Conditional 1: The Hypothetical (если бы + past, past + бы)
titleEnglish: Conditional 1: The Hypothetical (если бы + past, past + бы)
description: Russian builds the conditional out of past-tense forms plus the particle бы. One structure covers past, present, and future hypotheticals. The if-clause uses если бы; the result-clause uses бы after the verb.

title: Conditional 2: Polite Requests and Softening with бы
titleEnglish: Conditional 2: Polite Requests and Softening with бы
description: The бы particle is the most common politeness device in Russian. It turns a bare request into a polite one through three frames: я хотел(а) бы, the impersonal хотелось бы, and the most polite 'не могли бы вы + infinitive.'

title: Conditional 3: Counterfactual Want (я бы выпил, я бы пошёл)
titleEnglish: Conditional 3: Counterfactual Want (я бы выпил, я бы пошёл)
description: The 'subject + бы + past' frame on its own (no если-clause) expresses a current desire as a conditional wish. It is the everyday Russian way to say 'I'd have a coffee' or 'I would go for a walk' as a soft, conditional preference.

title: Conditional 4: The чтобы Complementizer (Purpose and Indirect Command)
titleEnglish: Conditional 4: The чтобы Complementizer (Purpose and Indirect Command)
description: Чтобы (a fused form of что + бы) introduces purpose clauses and indirect commands. It takes an infinitive when the subject is the same as the main clause, and a past-tense verb when the subject differs.

title: Conditional 6: Mixed Review
description: The closing review of the conditional track. For every sentence with бы, name which of the five uses is working, then produce the right form. No new material: a previous lesson covers the frozen idioms (как будто бы, лишь бы, что бы ни).

title: Conditional 5: Idiomatic бы Forms (как будто бы, лишь бы, что бы ни)
titleEnglish: Conditional 5: Idiomatic бы Forms (как будто бы, лишь бы, что бы ни)
description: Three frozen бы expressions B1 readers meet constantly: как будто бы (as if), лишь бы / только бы (if only / as long as), and что бы ни / кто бы ни / где бы ни (no matter what / who / where). Learn what each means and produce them.

title: Impersonal 1: Можно and Нельзя (permission and prohibition)
titleEnglish: Impersonal 1: Можно and Нельзя (permission and prohibition)
description: Russian builds permission and prohibition with two short words plus an infinitive. Можно says the action is allowed; нельзя says it is not. The person the rule applies to goes in the dative.

title: Impersonal 2: Нужно and Надо (necessity)
description: Russian builds everyday necessity with two near-synonyms: нужно and надо. The slot is the same as можно or нельзя: an optional dative person, the necessity word, and an infinitive. This lesson adds the не нужно / не надо soft negation and the past было / future будет tense words.

title: Impersonal 3: Advice (следует, стоит, лучше)
description: A softer modal family for giving advice. Следует is the formal 'ought to.' Стоит says the action is worth doing. Лучше is 'had better.' All three sit in the impersonal slot with a dative person plus an infinitive.

title: Impersonal 5: State Predicatives (холодно, грустно, трудно, важно)
titleEnglish: Impersonal 5: State Predicatives (холодно, грустно, трудно, важно)
description: Russian reports a state with a short adverb-shaped predicative and no nominative subject. Personal feelings name the person who feels it in the dative (Мне холодно); weather and atmospheric states often go without a person.

title: Impersonal 6: Reflexive Impersonals (хочется, кажется, удаётся)
description: A small family of verbs ending in -ся build impersonal sentences with no nominative subject. Хочется reports a soft feeling of wanting (compare the deliberate хочу). Кажется reports a tentative opinion. Удаётся reports a success. The structure: dative person (optional) + the reflexive verb in the 3rd-singular neuter form, often with a complement.

title: Impersonal 7: Mixed Review (the family diagnostic)
description: All seven families of impersonal constructions from this track brought together: permission, necessity, advice, timing, state, reflexive, and absence. A step-by-step diagnostic walks you through choosing and producing the right family for any context. Nothing new is taught.

title: Impersonal 4: Пора and Timing (it is time to)
titleEnglish: Impersonal 4: Пора and Timing (it is time to)
description: Пора announces that the moment for an action has arrived: Пора идти. With a verb of motion, the infinitive is often dropped and only the destination remains: Маше пора домой. Optional dative names whose moment it is.

title: Motion Verbs 1: идти vs ходить
description: The first motion-verb pair: walking. идти marks a single one-way trip in progress; ходить marks a round-trip, a habit, or a general ability.

title: Motion Verbs 2: ехать vs ездить
description: The transport pair. Ехать = single one-way trip in progress, by some vehicle. Ездить = round-trip, habit, or general claim about motion by vehicle.

title: Motion Verbs 3: Destinations with в and на
titleEnglish: Motion Verbs 3: Destinations with в and на
description: Motion verbs answer the question куда? with the accusative case. Enclosed spaces, buildings, cities, and countries take в + acc. Events, workplaces, and a fixed list of idiomatic places take на + acc.

title: Motion Verbs 4: Prefix по- (set off)
description: The prefix по- attaches to идти / ехать and turns the verb perfective. The new meaning is the onset of motion: the moment of setting off, leaving, or heading for a destination. Past forms only at this stage.

title: Motion Verbs 5: Prefix при- (arrive)
description: The prefix при- attaches to идти / ехать and turns the verb perfective. The new meaning is arrival: the moment the subject reaches the destination. Past forms only at this stage.

title: Motion Verbs 6: Prefix у- (gone away)
description: The prefix у- attaches to идти / ехать and turns the verb perfective. The new meaning is 'gone away from the speaker's location': the subject is no longer here. Past forms only at this stage.

title: Motion Verbs 7: Prefix вы- (step out)
description: The prefix вы- attaches to идти / ехать and turns the verb perfective. The new meaning is exiting a specific bounded space: a room, a building, a vehicle, a tunnel. Compare with у- from Lesson 6, which marks the broader 'gone away' reading.

title: Motion Verbs 8: Prefix в- (step into) and the ъ spelling
titleEnglish: Motion Verbs 8: Prefix в- (step into) and the ъ spelling
description: The prefix в- attaches to идти / ехать and turns the verb perfective, with the meaning of stepping into a bounded space. Choose вошёл / въехал for crossing a threshold (vs при- for plain arrival), and spell въехал with the hard sign ъ.

title: Motion Verbs 9: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis of the motion-verb track. The pair-choice (one-way vs round-trip), the destination preposition (в / на + acc), and all five prefixes (по-, при-, у-, вы-, в-) come together. The student names the framework operating in each sentence and builds full motion sentences.

title: Motion Verbs 10: The Rest of the Family (run, fly, carry)
titleEnglish: Motion Verbs 10: The Rest of the Family (run, fly, carry)
description: The same one-way / round-trip split you drilled on идти/ходить and ехать/ездить runs through the rest of the family: бежать/бегать, лететь/летать, плыть/плавать, plus the transitive carrying verbs нести, вести, везти.

title: Motion Verbs 11: Frozen Motion-Verb Idioms (recognition)
description: Four fixed expressions reuse a prefixed motion verb with a non-motion meaning: выходить замуж (a woman gets married), прийти в себя (regain consciousness), заходить в гости (drop in), переходить на ты (switch to first-name terms). Learn them as whole units.

title: Numerals 1: один Agrees Like an Adjective
titleEnglish: Numerals 1: один Agrees Like an Adjective
description: The number 1 (один/одна/одно/одни) changes to match the gender of its noun, and the noun stays in its plain dictionary form: один стол, одна книга, одно окно.

title: Numerals 2: 2, 3, 4 Take the Genitive Singular
description: After 2, 3, and 4 (and оба/обе), the noun goes into the genitive singular: две книги, три брата, четыре окна. Два/две splits by gender.

title: Numerals 3: 5 and Up Take the Genitive Plural
titleEnglish: Numerals 3: 5 and Up Take the Genitive Plural
description: After 5 and every higher number, the noun goes into the genitive plural: пять книг, шесть братьев, десять окон. This is the form where endings shorten or disappear.

title: Numerals 4: Compound Numbers - the Last Word Decides
titleEnglish: Numerals 4: Compound Numbers - the Last Word Decides
description: In a compound number like 21, 32, or 105, only the LAST word governs the noun: двадцать один стол, двадцать два стола, двадцать пять столов.

title: Numerals 5: When the Number Itself Declines
titleEnglish: Numerals 5: When the Number Itself Declines
description: In any case other than the nominative (dative, instrumental, prepositional) the numeral two, three, four, five takes its own case ending: к двум, с тремя, о пяти. Learn the forms with concrete everyday frames.

title: Numerals 6: Collective Numbers (двое, трое, четверо)
description: Collective numerals двое, трое, четверо count people as a group and pair with paired or plural-only nouns. They take the genitive plural: двое детей, трое друзей, четверо суток.

title: Numerals 7: Money, Age, and Time
description: Apply the 1 / 2-4 / 5+ split to the most common counted nouns: рубль (рубль / рубля / рублей), год (год / года / лет), and час (час / часа / часов).

title: Numerals 8: Mixed Review in Context
description: Bring lessons 1-7 together: the 1 / 2-4 / 5+ split, compound numbers, numerals in non-nominative cases, collective numerals, and money / age / time, all in realistic sentences.

title: Numerals 9: Irregular Numerals (полтора, оба/обе, год → лет)
titleEnglish: Numerals 9: Irregular Numerals (полтора, оба/обе, год → лет)
description: The low-numeral irregulars you have to produce: год/года/лет, полтора/полторы (with the single non-nominative полутора), and the full declension of оба/обе with its gender split.

title: Numerals 10: Large Numbers (сорок, девяносто, сто, тысяча, миллион)
titleEnglish: Numerals 10: Large Numbers (сорок, девяносто, сто, тысяча, миллион)
description: The big-number anomalies: the flat сорок/девяносто/сто (two forms only) and the noun-like тысяча/миллион, which force the genitive plural on the following noun in every case.

title: Plural 1: From One to Many
description: Form the regular nominative plural: hard stems take -ы, soft stems take -и, neuter swaps -о to -а and -е to -я, and after к, г, х, ж, ш, ч, щ the ending is always -и.

title: Plural 2: Accusative and the Animacy Split
titleEnglish: Plural 2: Accusative and the Animacy Split
description: In the plural, the accusative depends on animacy. Inanimate plurals reuse the nominative plural; animate plurals borrow the genitive plural. The split applies to all three genders, not just to masculines as in the singular.

title: Plural 3: Masculine Genitive (-ов / -ев / -ей)
description: The masculine genitive plural splits three ways. Hard consonants take -ов, soft -й takes -ев, and soft -ь plus ж, ш, ч, щ all take -ей. Triggered by numbers 5+, by нет, много, мало, несколько, and by genitive prepositions.

title: Plural 4: Feminine and Neuter Genitive (zero ending and -ей)
titleEnglish: Plural 4: Feminine and Neuter Genitive (zero ending and -ей)
description: The feminine and neuter genitive plural relies on a different mechanic. Hard fem -а and hard neuter -о drop their vowel to a zero ending, often inserting a fleeting -о- or -е- to break a consonant cluster. Soft fem -ь and soft neuter -е take -ей. The 3rd-declension feminine line takes -ей as well.

title: Plural 5: Dative (-ам / -ям)
description: After the difficulty of the plural genitive, the plural dative is a relief. One ending across all three genders, written -ам after hard stems and -ям after soft stems. Triggered by помогать, к + dat, по + dat (habitual), and the other dative-taking verbs you already know.

title: Plural 6: Instrumental (-ами / -ями)
description: The plural instrumental keeps the gentler dative pattern: one ending across all three genders. Hard stems take -ами, soft stems take -ями. Triggered by с + instr (accompaniment), bare instr (tools), the verbs гордиться / интересоваться, and the four position prepositions за / под / над / перед.

title: Plural 7: Prepositional (-ах / -ях)
description: The plural prepositional has one ending across all three genders: -ах after hard stems, -ях after soft stems. Always after a preposition: в, на, о / об, при.

title: Plural 8: All Six Cases Together
description: A mixed review of the regular plural endings across all six cases (lessons 1-7). Pick the right plural form for the job, name the case at work, and produce a few forms yourself. No new material.

title: Plural 9: Irregular Stems (дома, братья, дети / люди)
titleEnglish: Plural 9: Irregular Stems (дома, братья, дети / люди)
description: The three families whose plural STEM is unexpected: stress-shifted -а́ masculines (дома́, города́), the -ья family (бра́тья, друзья́), and the completely different words де́ти / лю́ди across all six cases.

title: Plural 10: Plural-Only Nouns and the -анин / -янин Family
titleEnglish: Plural 10: Plural-Only Nouns and the -анин / -янин Family
description: Two more irregular groups: nouns that exist only in the plural (часы́, но́жницы, де́ньги), whose genitive plural you must memorise, and the -анин / -янин nouns that drop -ин in the plural and take a zero genitive plural (англича́не → англича́н).

title: Plural 11: Irregular Plurals Mixed Review
description: A consolidation of all the irregular plural families from lessons 9 and 10: stress-shifted -а́, the -ья family, де́ти / лю́ди, plural-only nouns, and the -анин / -янин pattern. No new material - sort by family and produce the right form in context across the six cases.

title: Verbal Prefixes 1: The Concept (perfectivization plus a meaning shade)
titleEnglish: Verbal Prefixes 1: The Concept (perfectivization plus a meaning shade)
description: Russian builds new verbs by attaching prefixes to existing roots. The prefix typically perfectivizes the verb AND adds a meaning shade (across, until, out, completely, slightly, in). One root supports several prefixed verbs, each with its own meaning.

title: Verbal Prefixes 2: пере- (across, redo, over)
description: The prefix пере- covers three closely related shades: crossing across (перейти, переехать), redoing an action (перечитать, переделать, переписать), and exceeding a limit (переработать, перестараться). The shade is always recoverable from the verb root.

title: Verbal Prefixes 3: до- (until, up to, finish)
titleEnglish: Verbal Prefixes 3: до- (until, up to, finish)
description: The prefix до- adds 'finish what was started' or 'reach a goal / limit.' Дочитать = read to the end. Дойти = walk all the way to. Договориться = come to an agreement. The pattern is everywhere in B1 reading.

title: Verbal Prefixes 4: вы- (out, exhaust, complete)
description: The prefix вы- carries an 'outward' or 'completely done' shade: take out (вынести), drink up to the last drop (выпить), learn by heart (выучить), carry out a task (выполнить). The prefix usually steals stress in the past tense.

title: Verbal Prefixes 5: раз- / разо- (apart, completely, intensify)
titleEnglish: Verbal Prefixes 5: раз- / разо- (apart, completely, intensify)
description: The prefix раз- carries three shades: pulling apart (разделить, разорвать), completing fully (разбить, разогреть), and intensifying a process (разговориться, рассмеяться). The variant разо- appears before consonant clusters (разо- + й-: разошёлся).

title: Verbal Prefixes 6: при- (attach, slightly, bring along)
titleEnglish: Verbal Prefixes 6: при- (attach, slightly, bring along)
description: The prefix при- carries three closely related shades: arrival / attachment (привезти, привести, прийти), slightly / partly (приоткрыть, присесть), and bring-along / add-to (придумать, привезти подарок).

title: Verbal Prefixes 7: за- (start, beyond, achieve a state)
titleEnglish: Verbal Prefixes 7: за- (start, beyond, achieve a state)
description: The prefix за- carries three closely related shades: starting a process (запеть, заплакать, заговорить), dropping by a place along the way (зайти, заехать), and reaching a state by completing an action (закрыть, заплатить, заснуть).

title: Verbal Prefixes 8: Mixed Review with One Root, Many Prefixes
titleEnglish: Verbal Prefixes 8: Mixed Review with One Root, Many Prefixes
description: Synthesis of the prefix track. Same root + different prefixes give a family of perfectives with different meanings. The lesson asks the learner to NAME the prefix shade operating in each sentence and produce the matching form.

title: Prefix and Aspect 1: A Prefix Makes a Verb Perfective
titleEnglish: Prefix and Aspect 1: A Prefix Makes a Verb Perfective
description: A simplex imperfective verb plus a prefix usually becomes perfective. With a pure perfectivizing prefix the meaning stays the same; only the aspect changes. писать → написать, читать → прочитать, делать → сделать.

title: Prefix and Aspect 2: When the Prefix Adds Meaning Too
titleEnglish: Prefix and Aspect 2: When the Prefix Adds Meaning Too
description: A pure prefix only perfectivizes (писать → написать). Most prefixes perfectivize AND add a meaning shade (писать → переписать 'rewrite', дописать 'finish writing'). Both kinds make the verb perfective; the difference is whether the meaning changes.

title: Prefix and Aspect 3: Building the Secondary Imperfective
titleEnglish: Prefix and Aspect 3: Building the Secondary Imperfective
description: When a prefix adds meaning, its perfective gets a new imperfective built with the suffix -ыва-/-ива- (or -а-). переписать → переписывать, рассказать → рассказывать, открыть → открывать. This re-imperfectivized form is the secondary imperfective.

title: Prefix and Aspect 4: The Three-Step Ladder
titleEnglish: Prefix and Aspect 4: The Three-Step Ladder
description: One meaning gives three verb forms: simplex imperfective → prefixed perfective → secondary imperfective (писать → переписать → переписывать). The bottom and top are imperfective, the middle is perfective. Pick the rung your sentence needs.

title: Prefix and Aspect 5: Stem and Stress Changes
titleEnglish: Prefix and Aspect 5: Stem and Stress Changes
description: Forming the secondary imperfective often changes the stem: root о shifts to а (спросить → спрашивать), a consonant softens, and stress usually moves onto the syllable before -ыва-/-ива-. These adjustments are regular and few.

title: Prefix and Aspect 6: Mixed Review
description: Put the whole track together: a prefix perfectivizes, may add meaning, and a meaning-adding perfective rebuilds its imperfective with -ыва-/-ива-/-а- (with stem and stress changes). Pick the right rung of the ladder in real sentences.

title: Reported Speech 1: Что for Statements (keep the original tense)
titleEnglish: Reported Speech 1: Что for Statements (keep the original tense)
description: To report a statement, drop the quotation marks, link the clause with что after a comma, shift the pronoun to match the narrator, and keep the verb in the tense the speaker used.

title: Reported Speech 2: Ли for Yes/No Questions
titleEnglish: Reported Speech 2: Ли for Yes/No Questions
description: Russian reports a yes/no question with the particle ли. The word you are asking about moves to the front of the reported clause, and ли leans on it as the second word. The verb keeps its original tense.

title: Reported Speech 3: Q-Word Links for Content Questions
titleEnglish: Reported Speech 3: Q-Word Links for Content Questions
description: Russian reports a content question by reusing the original Q-word (кто, что, где, когда, почему, как) as the link word. No ли is added; the main verb decides whether что opens a statement or a question. Pronouns shift; tense is preserved.

title: Reported Speech 4: Чтобы for Commands and Requests
titleEnglish: Reported Speech 4: Чтобы for Commands and Requests
description: Russian reports a command, a request, or a wish-for-someone-else with чтобы followed by a past-form verb. When the speaker is also the doer, you use an infinitive instead. The choice depends on whether the two subjects match.

title: Reported Speech 5: Mixed Review (pick the right tool)
titleEnglish: Reported Speech 5: Mixed Review (pick the right tool)
description: All four reporting tools (что, ли, Q-word, чтобы) brought together in one review: pick the right linking word, shift the pronouns, and keep the speaker's original tense.

title: Indefinite 1: -то (Specific but Unknown)
description: The particle -то attaches to a question word (кто-то, что-то, где-то) to mean a real, specific referent that the speaker simply does not know or name. It lives in the past and in plain statements of fact.

title: Indefinite 2: -нибудь (Any, Not Yet Chosen)
description: The particle -нибудь (кто-нибудь, что-нибудь, где-нибудь) means 'any one at all, it doesn't matter which.' It lives in questions, requests, commands, the future, and hypotheticals, where the referent is still open.

title: Indefinite 3: -то vs -нибудь Head to Head
description: The core contrast of the track. -то marks a real, specific referent the speaker can't name (usually past, stated fact). -нибудь marks an open, not-yet-fixed one (questions, requests, future, conditions). Learn when each is required.

title: Indefinite 4: Negative ни- and Double Negation
titleEnglish: Indefinite 4: Negative ни- and Double Negation
description: Negative pronouns (никто, ничего, никогда, нигде, никакой) require a second negation on the verb: никто НЕ пришёл. The two negatives cooperate, not cancel. Stack as many as the sentence needs.

title: Indefinite 5: Declining Indefinite Pronouns
description: Indefinite pronouns decline by case. The question-word core (кто, что) takes the ending the verb or preposition demands, while the particle stays glued on: кого-то, кому-нибудь, с кем-то. With negatives, ни- splits around a preposition: ни с кем, ни о чём.

title: Indefinite 6: некого / нечего (No One / Nothing to ...)
titleEnglish: Indefinite 6: некого / нечего (No One / Nothing to ...)
description: The 'there is no one / nothing / nowhere / no time to do X' construction. Stress shifts to не- (нЕкого, not никогО), there is NO second не, the logical subject stands in the dative, and the verb is an infinitive: Мне нечего делать.

title: Indefinite 7: Mixed Review
description: The capstone of the track. Choose between -то, -нибудь, ни- + double negation, the correct case form, and the некого / нечего construction, all in one mixed set. This is where the whole indefinite-pronoun system comes together.

title: Participles 1: Active Present (-щий)
description: The Russian participle (причастие) is a verb-derived adjective. Today: the active present participle (the noun performs the action right now). Formation rule: 3rd-person plural minus ending plus -щ plus adjective endings.

title: Participles 2: Active Past (-вший / -ший)
description: The active past participle: the noun performed the action at some prior time. Today: formation from the past-tense stem; both aspects form this participle; irregular consonant-stem variants take -ший instead of -вший.

title: Participles 3: Passive Present (-мый)
description: The passive present participle: the noun is being acted upon right now. Today: formation from the 1st-person plural present (читаем + ый = читаемый), the -емый / -имый split, and the small fixed-expression core (любимый, уважаемый, изучаемый).

title: Participles 4: Passive Past Long Form - the -нный and -тый Families
titleEnglish: Participles 4: Passive Past Long Form - the -нный and -тый Families
description: The passive past participle in its long (attributive) form, for the two mechanical families: -нный from perfective -ать / -ять verbs (прочитанный, написанный) and -тый from monosyllabic stems and -ыть / -оть verbs (открытый, начатый). The -ить family comes in lesson 5.

title: Participles 6: Passive Past Short Form
description: The short form of the passive past participle: the predicative twin of the long form. Drop the final -ый and one of the doubled н to get the short form; it agrees in gender and number only (no case); the long-vs-short rule decides which form fits each slot.

title: Participles 7: Replacing Который Clauses
description: Russian writing converts a 'который + finite verb' clause into a participle phrase, and speech does the reverse. Today: the four conversion patterns, the position rule, and the non-nominative который that blocks conversion.

title: Participles 8: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis of all participle types from this track through one five-step diagnostic, including the -ить-family (-енн / -ённ) split. No new material - just consolidation and production.

title: Participles 5: Passive Past Long Form - the -ить Family (-енн / -ённ)
titleEnglish: Participles 5: Passive Past Long Form - the -ить Family (-енн / -ённ)
description: The third formation family: the passive past long form from perfective -ить verbs, choosing -енн- (stem stress: изу́ченный) vs -ённ- (suffix stress: решённый), and inserting the labial -л- after б в м п ф (купленный, поставленный).

title: Particles 1: же (Emphasis and Insistence)
description: The particle же adds emphasis, contrast, insistence, or the sense of 'the very same'. It sits right after the word it stresses and carries no dictionary meaning of its own; it tunes the speaker's stance.

title: Particles 2: ведь (Appeal to Shared Knowledge)
description: ведь appeals to what the speaker and listener both already know, like English 'after all', 'you know', or 'isn't it'. It justifies or reminds, expecting agreement. It is more flexible in position than же.

title: Particles 3: ли (Yes-No and Indirect Questions)
description: ли forms yes-no questions by fronting the focused word and attaching ли to it (Знаешь ли ты?). It is also the obligatory link in embedded indirect questions: Я не знаю, придёт ли он. ли leans on the word before it and never starts a clause.

title: Particles 4: разве and неужели (Surprise and Disbelief)
titleEnglish: Particles 4: разве and неужели (Surprise and Disbelief)
description: разве and неужели turn a statement into a question loaded with surprise or disbelief: 'Really?', 'You can't be serious'. неужели is pure astonishment; разве often expects 'no' and can sound doubtful or challenging. Both can carry rhetorical force.

title: Particles 5: emphatic -то (Topic and Concession)
description: The emphatic particle -то (written with a hyphen) attaches to a content word to spotlight it as the topic (Погода-то хорошая!), to concede a point before a 'but' (Сделать-то я сделал, но...), or to soften a statement. This is the emphatic -то, not the indefinite -то of кто-то / где-то.

title: Particles 7: Word Order and Stacking
description: Where particles sit. же and ли lean on the word in front of them and never begin a clause; ведь, вот, разве, неужели are freer and often lead. This lesson drills placement and the order in which particles stack.

title: Particles 8: Mixed Review
description: A capstone review of the whole track: choosing the right particle (же, ведь, ли, разве, неужели, -то, вот) by the speaker's intent, distinguishing the close pairs, placing the leaning particles correctly, and producing the forms yourself by translating from intent. The hardest skill is picking the function, not translating a word.

title: Particles 6: вот (Pointer and Spoken Filler)
description: вот is a pointing word: it presents something ('Вот мой дом'), names the key point ('Вот почему я опоздал'), and runs through speech as a filler ('Ну вот'). This lesson works one word, in those three jobs.

title: Subordination 1: который Basics
description: который ('who/which/that') connects a describing clause to a noun. Two steps: get gender and number from the noun, get case from the role inside the clause.

title: Subordination 2: который - Tricky Cases
description: The main clause's case does not transfer to который. Plus: dative after помочь, animate accusative = genitive, and other forms beyond the basics.

title: Subordination 3: который After Prepositions
description: When the role of который inside its clause involves a preposition, the preposition comes FIRST and который takes the case that preposition governs: дом, в котором я живу; друг, с которым я говорил; человек, о котором мы думаем.

title: Subordination 4: чтобы vs что
description: что reports a fact and takes an ordinary finite verb (Он сказал, что придёт). чтобы expresses purpose or desire and forces an infinitive or a past-tense verb, never a present or future (Я пришёл, чтобы помочь).

title: Subordination 5: чтобы + Past for a Different Subject
titleEnglish: Subordination 5: чтобы + Past for a Different Subject
description: The subject test for чтобы: same subject takes the bare infinitive (Я хочу прийти, I want to come), but a DIFFERENT subject takes чтобы + a past-tense verb (Я хочу, чтобы ты пришёл, I want you to come).

title: Subordination 6: Cause and Reason
description: Connect a result to its cause: потому что (because, answers why), так как / поскольку (since, fronted reason), поэтому (therefore, introduces the result), из-за того что (because of, negative cause), благодаря тому что (thanks to, positive cause).

title: Subordination 7: Concession and Condition
description: Concession (хотя, несмотря на то что - although / in spite of the fact that) marks a result that holds DESPITE an obstacle. Condition (если, в случае если - if / in the event that) marks a result that depends on something being true.

title: Subordination 8: Mixed Review
description: Bring the whole track together: который (agreement, case, and after prepositions), чтобы vs что, the subject test for чтобы, and the cause, concession, and condition connectors, all chosen and built in realistic sentences.

title: Verbal Adverbs 1: The Imperfective -я Form
description: The Russian verbal adverb (деепричастие) compresses a secondary action into one short word. Today: forming the imperfective -я / -а gerund from the third-person plural present.

title: Verbal Adverbs 2: Simultaneous Action
description: What the imperfective verbal adverb means: an action that runs at the same time as the main verb. Today: recognizing the simultaneous reading and rewriting когда clauses as gerund clauses.

title: Verbal Adverbs 3: The Perfective -в Form
description: The second verbal adverb type: the perfective form (-в for most verbs, -вшись for reflexives). Take the perfective infinitive, drop -ть, add the suffix.

title: Verbal Adverbs 4: Prior Completed Action
description: What the perfective verbal adverb means: an action completed BEFORE the main verb. Today: producing the form in real sentences and contrasting it with the imperfective.

title: Verbal Adverbs 5: The Same-Subject Rule
description: The most important constraint on Russian verbal adverbs: the gerund and the main verb must share a subject. Today: spotting dangling-gerund errors and rewriting them with когда clauses.

title: Verbal Adverbs 6: Style and the когда Choice
titleEnglish: Verbal Adverbs 6: Style and the когда Choice
description: Verbal adverbs are a written-register feature. Today: when to choose a gerund and when a когда clause is more natural, and how to chain several gerunds under one subject. Negation gets its own lesson next.

title: Verbal Adverbs 8: Mixed Review
description: Synthesis of the verbal adverb track: imperfective and perfective formation, simultaneous vs prior reading, the same-subject rule, register choice, and negation. Today: pull all five threads together and produce the full range.

title: Verbal Adverbs 7: Negating Gerunds with не
titleEnglish: Verbal Adverbs 7: Negating Gerunds with не
description: Negate a verbal adverb by placing не directly before it as a separate word (не зная, не понимая, не глядя), avoiding the незная fusion error, and choose the aspect of the negated gerund by timing.
